mots.sens: This term denotes an unconditional and selfless love, often associated with divine love. In this verse, it emphasizes the depth of Jesus' love for his disciples, a love that is manifested through concrete actions. Agapē is a love that goes beyond emotions, expressed through service and sacrifice, which is particularly relevant in the context of the Passion of Christ.

This verb means 'to arrive' or 'to be present,' and in this context, it refers to the appointed hour of Jesus to accomplish His saving mission. This underscores God's sovereignty over time and events, as well as Jesus' willingness to submit to this divine plan. Spiritually, it reminds us that every moment of our lives is under God's control.

This term refers to the world as a whole, often in contrast to the divine sphere. In the context of this verse, it highlights the reality in which Jesus carried out His ministry, a world often in rebellion against God. It reminds us that Christ's love extends to all, even in a world that rejects Him.

1.epoque: The passage is set in the first century, in a Jewish context where the Passover festival held central importance, symbolizing liberation and sacrifice. It is a period marked by religious and political tensions, with Jesus facing opposition from Jewish and Roman authorities.
1.passage: This verse is situated within the framework of Jesus' last meal with His disciples, a crucial moment before His crucifixion. It introduces the theme of Jesus' sacrificial love, which will be demonstrated by His act of washing His disciples' feet, thus illustrating service and humility.
1.culture: In Jewish culture, the Passover festival is a time of commemorating the liberation from Egypt, and it is laden with profound spiritual meanings. This context reinforces the idea that Jesus is the true Lamb of God, whose sacrifice will bring eternal liberation.
1.interpretation: This verse highlights Jesus' awareness of His imminent mission and the love He has for His disciples. It teaches us that true love is manifested in service and sacrifice, and that even in difficult moments, we must love and serve others.
1.commentaire: John 13:1 reminds us that Jesus' love is both deep and practical. In our lives, we are called to imitate this love by serving others, even in times of suffering or difficulty. By understanding the depth of this love, we are encouraged to live an active faith, demonstrating our commitment to God and to our neighbor.

mots.sens: This word means 'accuser' or 'slanderer.' It designates the spiritual enemy, Satan, who seeks to sow discord and divert hearts from the ways of God. In this verse, his role is crucial as he inspires Judas to betray Jesus, thus highlighting the spiritual struggle taking place in the human heart. The presence of the devil reminds believers of the necessity to remain vigilant against temptations.

This term refers to the 'heart,' not only as a physical organ but also as the center of emotions, thoughts, and wills. In Jewish culture, the heart is often seen as the seat of morality and spiritual decisions. The fact that Judas received inspiration in his heart highlights the gravity of his choices and the human capacity to turn away from God despite spiritual privileges.

This verb means 'to deliver' or 'to betray.' It implies a deliberate act of handing something over to another, often in a context of betrayal or renunciation. In the context of this verse, it underscores Judas' tragic choice to betray the Son of God, which has eternal consequences. It reminds us that our choices impact not only ourselves but also those around us.

2.epoque: The passage is set in the first century, during the earthly life of Jesus, as the tension between the Jewish religious authorities and Jesus intensifies.
2.passage: This verse is found within the context of the Last Supper, a crucial moment where Jesus shares His final moments with His disciples, teaching them profound truths before His imminent crucifixion.
2.culture: In Jewish culture, a shared meal held great significance, symbolizing intimacy and communion. Judas' betrayal during this sacred moment accentuates the gravity of his act.
2.interpretation: This verse illustrates the spiritual struggle between good and evil, highlighting how the devil can influence hearts. Judas' betrayal serves as a warning about human vulnerability to the influence of evil.
2.commentaire: This passage exhorts us to keep our hearts vigilant and to resist inspirations that lead us away from Christ. Like Judas, we can be exposed to devastating choices, but by remaining anchored in prayer and the Word of God, we can discern divine will and avoid falling into spiritual betrayal. Let us be attentive to our hearts and motivations, always seeking to honor our Lord.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to hand over,' 'to entrust,' or 'to deliver.' In the context of John 13:3, it emphasizes the authority and sovereignty of God, who entrusts all things to Jesus. This evokes a relationship of trust between the Father and the Son, where everything that belongs to God is placed in Jesus' hands, thus reinforcing His role as mediator and Savior.

This term means 'to go out' or 'to come forth.' In the context of this verse, it refers to the divine origin of Jesus, who came from God and is returning to Him. This underscores Jesus' divine mission and His return to the Father, which is central to understanding His redemptive work.

This verb means 'to know' or 'to understand.' In this passage, it indicates Jesus' perfect knowledge of His mission and identity. This knowledge is essential for understanding the divine nature of Jesus and His authority, as He acts in full awareness of His relationship with the Father.

This word means 'Father.' In the context of John 13:3, it emphasizes the intimate relationship between Jesus and God the Father. This relationship is fundamental in Christian theology, as it reveals the trinitarian nature of God and the perfect love that exists between the Father and the Son.

3.epoque: The passage is set in the first century, in the context of the Roman Empire, where society was marked by religious and political tensions.
3.passage: This verse is found within the framework of Jesus' last meal with His disciples, just before His crucifixion, where He prepares His disciples for His imminent death and teaches them humility through the washing of feet.
3.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, the role of a servant was often seen as lowly, but Jesus overturns this perception by showing that true greatness is found in service and humility.
3.interpretation: This verse reveals Jesus' full awareness of His divine identity and mission. He knows that He is the Son of God, sent to fulfill the Father's will, which gives Him the confidence and authority necessary to serve and sacrifice His life for humanity.
3.commentaire: John 13:3 reminds us that Jesus, as the Son of God, has all power and authority, yet He chooses to serve others. This teaches us that true greatness lies in humility and service. By imitating Christ's example, we are called to serve our neighbors with love and devotion, thus reflecting God's love in our daily lives.

mots.sens: This word means 'to rise' and is often used in the New Testament to denote an action of movement or change of position. In this context, it symbolizes the transition from a position of master to that of servant, highlighting Jesus' humility. The root of this word also evokes resurrection, reinforcing the idea that service and humility are at the heart of Christ's mission.

This term means 'to take off' or 'to strip' and refers to the action of undressing. In the context of this verse, it illustrates Jesus' willingness to strip off his garments, symbolizing the renunciation of his rights and status. Theologically, this underscores the principle of incarnation, where Jesus becomes a servant for the salvation of humanity.

This word refers to a 'cloth' or 'belt', often used to gird oneself for a task or service. In the narrative, Jesus takes a belt to prepare to wash the feet of his disciples, which is an act of service. This emphasizes the idea that service is an essential characteristic of Christian leadership.

4.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, in the context of Palestine under Roman rule, where social relations were marked by strict hierarchies and well-defined roles.
4.passage: John 13 takes place during the last meal of Jesus with his disciples, a crucial moment before his crucifixion. This chapter highlights Jesus' teaching on humility and service, illustrated by the act of washing his disciples' feet.
4.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, foot washing was a task reserved for servants, emphasizing humility and devotion. This act of Jesus overturns social norms and redefines leadership.
4.interpretation: Jesus' act of rising, undressing, and girding himself with a cloth is a powerful illustration of his love and service. It reminds us that true greatness in the kingdom of God is manifested through humility and serving others.
4.commentaire: This verse calls us to adopt a servant's attitude in our daily lives. By imitating Jesus' example, we are invited to renounce our rights and serve others with love and humility. It encourages us to see every opportunity for service as a chance to reflect the character of Christ.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to wash' or 'to rinse'. In the context of John 13:5, it evokes the action of cleaning feet, a humble act of service. The root of this word is related to purification, which underscores the importance of spiritual and physical cleanliness. Theologically, this act of foot washing by Jesus symbolizes service, humility, and the necessity of being purified to be in communion with God.

This term refers to a 'cloth' or 'garment'. In the context of this verse, it refers to the cloth used by Jesus to wipe the feet of the disciples. This word highlights the idea of a servant, as Jesus uses a simple garment to accomplish a humble task. Spiritually, it illustrates how Christ, though Lord, becomes a servant to teach love and humility.

This word means 'basin' or 'container'. In this passage, it represents the place where water is held for washing feet. The notion of a basin evokes purification and renewal, emphasizing the importance of this act within the community of disciples. Theologically, it reminds us that Christ is the source of purification for his disciples.

5.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, in the context of Palestine under Roman occupation, where practices of purification and hospitality were essential in Jewish culture.
5.passage: John 13 is part of Jesus' farewell discourse before his crucifixion, where he teaches his disciples the importance of service and mutual love.
5.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, foot washing was an act reserved for servants, making Jesus' action all the more remarkable and significant.
5.interpretation: Jesus' act of washing the feet of his disciples is a powerful illustration of humility and service. It teaches that to be great in the kingdom of God, one must be willing to serve others.
5.commentaire: This passage calls us to adopt a posture of humility and service towards others, following Christ's example. As disciples, we are called to wash one another's feet, symbolizing our commitment to love and serve our neighbor, while reminding us that true leadership is manifested through service.

mots.sens: This term means 'Lord' and is used to denote supreme authority. In the biblical context, it evokes not only the sovereignty of God but also the relationship of allegiance and respect that believers should have towards Christ. Peter's use of this word emphasizes the recognition of Jesus as the Messiah and the Son of God, highlighting the tension between divine authority and the humility of service.

This word means 'to wash' and refers to an act of purification. In Jewish culture, foot washing was a task reserved for servants, symbolizing humility and service. Jesus' action of washing the feet of his disciples illustrates the servant nature of Christ and his call to his disciples to serve others, even in the most humble tasks.

6.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, in the context of Palestine occupied by the Romans, where social relations were marked by strict hierarchies and deep Jewish religious practices.
6.passage: John 13 takes place during the last meal of Jesus with his disciples before his crucifixion. This chapter highlights Jesus' teaching on humility and service, culminating in the act of washing his disciples' feet.
6.culture: In Jewish and Roman culture, foot washing was a common practice to welcome guests, but it was generally performed by servants. This act of Jesus overturns the social and cultural norms of the time.
6.interpretation: Peter, exclaiming, 'You, Lord, wash my feet!', expresses a misunderstanding of Jesus' humility. This moment reveals the depth of Christ's love, who does not merely claim his authority but chooses to serve, thus showing that true greatness lies in selfless service.
6.commentaire: This verse reminds us that leadership in the kingdom of God is manifested through service and humility. Just as Jesus washed the feet of his disciples, we are called to serve those around us, regardless of their status. By imitating this example, we bear witness to Christ's love and our commitment to live according to his teachings.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to know' or 'to understand'. It expresses a knowledge that goes beyond intellectual information to include personal and relational experience. In this verse, it emphasizes that Peter's understanding is limited to the present moment, but it will be deepened in the future, thus revealing the progression of divine revelation in the lives of believers.

This word means 'to come' or 'to arrive'. It carries the idea of movement towards a goal or destination. In the context of this verse, it evokes the notion that Peter's understanding will not be realized immediately, but will come to him in a future time, thus highlighting God's patience and sovereignty in the process of revelation.

7.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, during the earthly ministry of Jesus, at a time when the disciples were still discovering the full scope of his teaching and mission.
7.passage: John 13 is part of Jesus' farewell discourse, where he teaches his disciples profound truths before his crucifixion. This moment is crucial as it prepares the disciples for the reality of his death and resurrection.
7.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, foot washing was an act of humility, often reserved for servants. By performing this act, Jesus overturns social norms and shows that service is at the heart of his mission.
7.interpretation: Jesus' statement to Peter emphasizes that spiritual understanding is often progressive. The disciples, like us today, may not immediately grasp God's plans, but they are called to trust in his wisdom and timing.
7.commentaire: This verse reminds us that our understanding of God and his ways may be limited in the present moment. We are encouraged to trust God even when we do not fully understand his actions. In the meantime, we must remain open to the future revelation that He will give us, as each experience of faith brings us closer to his truth.

mots.sens: The Greek word 'lysis' means 'deliverance' or 'liberation'. In the context of John 13:8, it evokes the idea of spiritual purification and cleansing. Jesus uses this term to emphasize that foot washing is a metaphor for the necessity of being purified to have a relationship with him. The theological implication here is that without this purification, one cannot participate in communion with Christ.

The term 'meros' translates to 'part' or 'portion'. It designates a share that is assigned or a participation in something greater. In this verse, Jesus emphasizes that without the washing, Peter cannot have a part with him, thus indicating the importance of purification for entering into divine communion. It also highlights the necessity of humility and acceptance of God's grace.

8.epoque: In Jesus' time, foot washing was a common practice, especially in Eastern cultures where people walked barefoot on dusty roads. This reflects a social hierarchy, as this service was generally reserved for slaves.
8.passage: This passage is set in the context of Jesus' last meal with his disciples, where he teaches profound lessons about service, humility, and the necessity of spiritual purification. John 13 is a key chapter that introduces the theme of service and Christ's unconditional love.
8.culture: In Jewish and Roman culture, foot washing was an act of hospitality and respect. By washing his disciples' feet, Jesus overturns social norms and shows that true leadership is manifested through service.
8.interpretation: The interaction between Jesus and Peter reveals human resistance to accepting divine grace and purification. Jesus insists that foot washing is essential for having a part with him, which underscores the importance of humility and submission to his redemptive work.
8.commentaire: This verse teaches us that to enter into communion with Christ, we must first accept his purification. It reminds us that our own pride or refusal to accept grace can distance us from our relationship with him. As Christians, we are called to serve others with humility, following the example of our Lord.

mots.sens: This word means 'rock' and is the name given to Simon by Jesus. It symbolizes the solidity and foundation of the Church. In this context, Peter expresses a deep understanding of spiritual purification, recognizing that foot washing is just one part of the necessary purification to be in communion with Christ.

This term means 'Lord' and denotes supreme authority. In the New Testament, it is often used to acknowledge the divinity of Jesus. Peter's use of this word underscores his respect and submission to Jesus, while revealing an understanding of the necessity of complete purification.

This word means 'hand' and symbolizes action and service. In the context of this verse, it represents Peter's desire to be fully purified to serve the Lord. This shows an understanding of the importance of sanctification in the Christian life.

This term means 'head' and can symbolize authority and position. By asking for his head to be washed as well, Peter expresses a desire for total purification, encompassing not only his service but also his spirit and thoughts. This underscores the importance of fully submitting to Christ in all aspects of life.

9.epoque: The historical context of this passage is set in the first century, during the earthly life of Jesus, as he teaches his disciples before his crucifixion. It was a time of religious and political tensions in Israel, with a strong messianic expectation among the Jewish people.
9.passage: This verse is found in chapter 13 of the Gospel of John, which describes Jesus' last meal with his disciples. This moment is marked by Jesus' humility as he washes the feet of his disciples, illustrating service and unconditional love.
9.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, foot washing was a task reserved for servants. This highlights the humility and service that Jesus sought to teach his disciples, challenging established social and religious norms.
9.interpretation: The interaction between Jesus and Peter highlights the limited human understanding of spiritual purification. Peter, by asking for a complete washing, demonstrates a desire for closeness with Christ, but he does not yet fully understand the nature of the purification that Jesus offers.
9.commentaire: This verse reminds us that spiritual purification goes beyond external rituals; it involves a total commitment to Christ. Like Peter, we are called to desire complete purification, not only in our actions but also in our thoughts and hearts. By serving others with humility, we imitate Jesus' example and live our faith authentically.

mots.sens: The word 'katharos' means 'pure' or 'clean'. In the biblical context, it evokes a spiritual purification, often associated with holiness and separation from sin. The root of this word is linked to the idea of being free from any defilement, both physical and moral. In this verse, it emphasizes the importance of the inner purification that Jesus offers, while acknowledging that some are not yet purified.

The term 'nipto' refers to the action of washing or cleansing oneself, often in reference to a partial washing. In the context of this passage, it underscores the necessity of maintaining continuous purity even after an initial cleansing. This word is used to describe the washing of feet, symbolizing the need to rid oneself of the impurities accumulated in our daily walk with the Lord.

The word 'pas' means 'all' or 'each'. It is used to indicate universality or totality. In this verse, it emphasizes that, although the disciples are largely purified, there is an exception that requires special attention. This reminds us that purification is an ongoing process and that each person must examine their own heart.

10.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, in the context of Roman-occupied Palestine, where Jewish religious practices were flourishing and Jesus was teaching His disciples about the true nature of service and humility.
10.passage: John 13 is part of the account of the Last Supper, where Jesus, before His crucifixion, teaches His disciples the importance of humility and service through the washing of feet. This chapter highlights the relationships between Jesus and His disciples, as well as the imminent betrayal by Judas.
10.culture: In Jewish culture, foot washing was a common practice for purification before eating or when welcoming guests. It also symbolized humility, as it was a service typically reserved for slaves.
10.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that, although the disciples have been purified by the word of Jesus, they must continue to wash their feet, symbolizing the necessity of regularly repenting and purifying themselves in their walk with God. It reminds us that sanctification is an ongoing process in the believer's life.
10.commentaire: Jesus teaches here that initial purification is essential, but it must be followed by constant vigilance to remain in communion with Him. As Christians, we are called to recognize our impurities and seek daily purification through prayer and repentance. This passage encourages us to remain in the light of Christ, in order to live a life that is pleasing to Him.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to deliver' or 'to hand over'. In the context of John 13:11, it refers to the act of Judas Iscariot betraying Jesus. The root of this word evokes the idea of entrusting something to someone, often with a connotation of betrayal. Theologically, this underscores the depth of Judas's betrayal and Jesus's perfect knowledge of human nature, which highlights God's grace and mercy in the face of sin.

This term means 'pure' or 'clean'. In the context of this verse, it refers to spiritual and moral purity. The root of this word is often associated with the idea of separation from evil and consecration to God. Spiritually, it reminds us that Jesus knows our hearts and our spiritual state, and that purity is essential for communion with Him.

This verb means 'to know' or 'to understand'. In this verse, it indicates the deep and intimate knowledge that Jesus has of Judas and his betrayal. This word is often used in the New Testament to signify a knowledge that goes beyond intellect, involving relational understanding. It underscores the divinity of Christ, who knows the hearts and intentions of men.

11.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, during Jesus's ministry in Palestine, a period marked by religious and political tensions between Jews and Romans.
11.passage: John 13 describes the last meal of Jesus with His disciples before His crucifixion. This chapter highlights the humility of Jesus as He washes the feet of His disciples, while revealing the hearts of those around Him.
11.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, foot washing was an act of servitude, reserved for the lowest servants. This underscores the humility of Jesus and His call for His disciples to serve others.
11.interpretation: Jesus, by declaring that 'you are not all clean', highlights the reality of betrayal among His close ones. This reminds us that even in a context of closeness to Christ, hearts can be far from Him.
11.commentaire: This verse teaches us the importance of spiritual authenticity. Jesus, knowing the condition of each disciple, reminds us that the purity of heart is essential for a true relationship with Him. As believers, we must examine our own hearts and ensure that we walk in the light, being aware of our need for God's grace.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to wash' or 'to cleanse oneself', and it is often associated with purification rituals. In the context of John 13:12, it emphasizes the act of humility and service that Jesus performs by washing the feet of His disciples. Spiritually, it evokes the necessity of purifying oneself and preparing to serve others, by imitating the example of Christ.

This term means 'to humble' or 'to lower', and it is related to the idea of humility. In this verse, it reflects the attitude of Jesus who, although being the Master, chooses to serve His disciples. The theological significance here is that true leadership in the kingdom of God is manifested through service and humility.

This verb means 'to understand' or 'to perceive', and it implies a deep understanding that goes beyond mere intellectual knowledge. In the context of John 13:12, Jesus asks His disciples if they grasp the meaning of His act, inviting them to reflect on their own attitude towards service and humility. This underscores the importance of spiritually grasping the lessons that Jesus teaches through His actions.

12.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, during the earthly life of Jesus, in a Jewish context where purification rituals and master-disciple relationships were very present.
12.passage: John 13 takes place during the last meal of Jesus with His disciples, a crucial moment where He teaches them profound truths before His crucifixion. This chapter highlights the love and service that Jesus embodies.
12.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, foot washing was a task reserved for servants, thus highlighting the humility required to serve others. Jesus, by performing this task, overturns social expectations and redefines leadership.
12.interpretation: Jesus's act of washing the feet of His disciples is a powerful metaphor for the love and service that every believer is called to manifest. It reminds us that the true disciple is one who serves others with humility and devotion.
12.commentaire: This verse calls us to reflect on our own attitude of service towards others. By imitating Christ, who lowered Himself to serve, we are invited to live an active and engaged faith, where humility and service become the marks of our discipleship. By understanding what Jesus has done, we are also called to act similarly in our daily lives.

mots.sens: This term means 'teacher' or 'master.' In the Jewish context, it refers to a person with the authority to teach the law and wisdom. The theological significance here emphasizes that Jesus, as Master, holds divine truth and guides his disciples in the knowledge of God.

This word translates to 'Lord' and implies a position of supreme authority. In the Old Testament, it is often used to refer to God himself. The recognition of Jesus as Lord in this verse highlights his divine authority and central role in the relationship between God and humanity.

13.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, in the context of Palestine under Roman occupation, where Jesus' teachings sparked both admiration and controversy among the Jews and Roman authorities.
13.passage: John 13 takes place during the last meal of Jesus with his disciples, where he teaches them profound lessons about service, humility, and love. This verse underscores the disciples' recognition of Jesus' identity as their Master and Lord.
13.culture: In Jewish culture, respect for teachers and authority figures was paramount. Disciples followed their master not only to learn but also to imitate his life and values.
13.interpretation: By presenting himself as Master and Lord, Jesus establishes a clear relationship between himself and his disciples, based on authority and teaching. This reminds us that our commitment to him must be based on a recognition of his divine authority and a desire to learn from him.
13.commentaire: This verse calls us to fully recognize Jesus as our Master and Lord in our daily lives. By accepting his authority, we are invited to follow him with obedience and to apply his teachings in our actions. This compels us to live an authentic faith, where our relationship with Christ influences every aspect of our existence.

mots.sens: This word means 'Lord' or 'Master.' It is used to denote a supreme authority, often in reference to God or Jesus Christ. In the context of John 13:14, it emphasizes Jesus' position as Lord who, despite his authority, becomes a servant. This highlights the paradoxical nature of Christian leadership, which is founded on humility and service.

This verb means 'to wash' or 'to cleanse oneself.' It is often used in the context of ritual purification, but here it takes on a strong symbolic dimension. By washing the feet, Jesus illustrates the act of humility and service that each disciple is called to practice. It also evokes the necessity of purifying one another within the Christian community.

This term means 'one another' and emphasizes the interconnectedness and mutual responsibility among members of the Christian community. It reflects the idea that love and service are not isolated acts but must be lived in relation to others. It also indicates that each Christian has an active role in supporting and building up others.

14.epoque: The passage is set in the 1st century, during Jesus' earthly ministry, in a context where social relationships were marked by strict hierarchies and defined roles.
14.passage: John 13 describes the last meal of Jesus with his disciples, where he teaches them humility and service through the washing of feet, an act reserved for servants.
14.culture: In the Jewish and Roman culture of the time, foot washing was a humiliating task, often performed by slaves. Jesus overturns this social norm by humbling himself to teach a profound lesson about service.
14.interpretation: This verse reminds us that true leadership in the kingdom of God is manifested through service and humility. By washing the feet of his disciples, Jesus establishes a model of Christian living where everyone is called to serve others, regardless of their status.
14.commentaire: John 13:14 calls us to adopt a servant attitude toward our brothers and sisters in Christ. By imitating Jesus' example, we are invited to actively engage in acts of service and humility, thereby strengthening the bonds within the Christian community. This passage reminds us that our faith must translate into concrete actions of love and mutual support.

mots.sens: This term means 'example' or 'model.' It evokes the idea of a tangible illustration to follow. In the context of this verse, Jesus presents himself as the perfect model of service and humility, urging his disciples to imitate his behavior. The theological significance of this word underscores the importance of imitating Christ in the believer's life.

This verb means 'to do' or 'to act.' It implies a deliberate and conscious action. In this verse, it calls the disciples not only to observe Jesus' example but to embody it in their own lives. This emphasizes the importance of putting Christ's teachings into practice in the daily lives of believers.

15.epoque: This verse is set in a historical context where Jesus, shortly before his crucifixion, teaches his disciples during the Last Supper, a crucial moment in the revelation of his ministry and imminent sacrifice.
15.passage: In John 13, Jesus washes the feet of his disciples, an act of service and humility, thus showing the importance of serving others. This chapter highlights the nature of Christian leadership, which is based on service rather than domination.
15.culture: In Jesus' time, foot washing was a task reserved for servants, highlighting the depth of humility and service that Jesus embodies. This overturns cultural norms of power and status, inviting a new vision of leadership.
15.interpretation: Jesus' invitation to 'do as he has done' is a call to live a life of selfless service. It reminds us that true greatness in the kingdom of God is measured by our ability to serve others with love and humility.
15.commentaire: This verse exhorts us to follow Christ's example in our daily lives. By imitating his humility and service, we reflect his love in our community. May our attitude be that of a servant, seeking to uplift others and live according to the values of the kingdom of God.

mots.sens: This word means 'servant' or 'slave' and evokes a relationship of submission and devotion. In the biblical context, it refers to the idea of serving with faithfulness and humility, which is essential in the Christian life. The theological significance of this term emphasizes that true leadership is manifested in service, following the example of Christ.

This term means 'lord' and indicates supreme authority. It is used to refer to God or Christ, highlighting their position of sovereignty. In this verse, it reminds us that even those sent by the Lord must recognize their place in the divine hierarchy and their dependence on Him.

The word 'apostle' means 'sent one' and refers to those who are called to carry a message or mission. It implies responsibility and a divine mandate. In the context of this verse, it reminds us that even those sent by Christ must remain humble and aware of their role as servants.

16.epoque: In the first century, the Jewish and Roman worlds valued social status and authority. Jesus' teachings contrasted with these norms by advocating humility and service.
16.passage: This verse is set in the context of Jesus' last meal with his disciples, where he teaches them the importance of service and humility, just after washing their feet.
16.culture: In Jewish culture, service was often associated with submission, but Jesus overturns this notion by showing that the true leader is the one who serves others.
16.interpretation: This verse reminds us that greatness in the kingdom of God is not measured by power or authority, but by our ability to serve others. It calls us to adopt an attitude of humility and to follow Christ's example.
16.commentaire: As Christians, we are called to be servants, imitating Jesus in our daily lives. This passage encourages us not to seek recognition or status, but to focus on selfless service to others, thereby reflecting Christ's love in our actions.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to know' or 'to understand.' It implies a knowledge that goes beyond mere intellectual information, encompassing a deep understanding and personal relationship. In the context of John 13:17, it emphasizes the importance of knowing Jesus' teachings not only as theological truths but as principles to live by daily.

This word translates to 'blessed' or 'happy.' It evokes a state of happiness that comes from divine favor and the fulfillment of God's will. In this verse, it emphasizes that true happiness is found in practicing Christ's teachings, not merely in theoretical knowledge.

This verb means 'to do' or 'to practice.' It implies a concrete action and a commitment to implement what one knows. In John 13:17, it is essential to understand that the promised happiness is conditioned by action, highlighting that faith must be expressed through works.

17.epoque: The passage is set in the first century, during a time when Jesus was teaching his disciples just before his crucifixion, in a cultural context deeply rooted in law and traditions.
17.passage: John 13 describes Jesus' last meal with his disciples, where he teaches them profound lessons about service and humility, notably by washing their feet, an act that illustrates the model of Christian leadership.
17.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, foot washing was a task reserved for servants, highlighting Jesus' humility and his call for his disciples to serve others with the same spirit.
17.interpretation: This verse reminds us that knowledge of spiritual truths must lead to concrete actions. The happiness promised by Jesus is linked to the practice of his teachings, emphasizing that living faith is manifested through works.
17.commentaire: John 13:17 urges us not to be content with merely knowing Christ's teachings, but to actively live them out. By practicing these truths, we experience the joy and blessing that God desires for us. Thus, our commitment to serve and love others becomes an authentic expression of our faith.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to choose' or 'to elect.' In the biblical context, it evokes the idea of divine selection, where God chooses individuals for a specific purpose. This underscores God's sovereignty in choosing his disciples, revealing that faith is not solely the result of human choice, but also of divine initiative. Spiritually, this reminds believers that they are called by God and have a mission to fulfill.

This term refers to 'bread' and symbolizes communion and relationship. In the context of the shared meal, it represents not only physical nourishment but also the spiritual communion between Jesus and his disciples. Theologically, it evokes the notion of covenant and betrayal, highlighting that sharing bread can also be an act of closeness before the breaking of trust.

This verb means 'to lift the heel' and is an expression that evokes rebellion or betrayal. In this verse, it refers to the act of Judas, who, despite his closeness to Jesus, chooses to betray him. Spiritually, this highlights the struggle between fidelity and betrayal, and how even those who are close to Christ can drift away from him.

18.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, during a time when Jesus was on his earthly mission, teaching and preparing his disciples for the upcoming events, including his crucifixion.
18.passage: John 13 takes place during Jesus' last meal with his disciples, where he announces his betrayal and establishes the model of service and humility through the washing of feet.
18.culture: In Jewish culture, sharing a meal was an act of communion and trust. Bread, as a central element of the meal, symbolized unity and relationship among the diners.
18.interpretation: This verse emphasizes Jesus' intimate knowledge of his disciples and the reality of the looming betrayal. It reminds us that even in moments of spiritual closeness, choices can lead to a separation from communion with God.
18.commentaire: This passage invites us to reflect on our own faithfulness to Christ. Just as Jesus knew Judas' betrayal, he knows our hearts and intentions. Let us be vigilant in our walk with him, seeking to nurture our relationship through prayer and the study of the Word, so that we remain steadfast in our commitment to him.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to say' or 'to speak', and it is often used in the New Testament to indicate an important statement or divine revelation. In this context, Jesus announces a truth that prepares his disciples to understand his identity and mission. The theological significance here is that the word of Christ is both prophetic and revealing, thereby strengthening the faith of believers.

This verb means 'to believe' or 'to have faith', and it is central to the evangelical message. It implies not only an intellectual belief but also a total trust in the person of Jesus. In this verse, faith is linked to the recognition of Christ's divine identity, emphasizing the importance of believing in him for salvation.

This verb means 'to come' or 'to arrive', and it is often used to describe the action of God or Christ entering into human history. Here, it refers to the future event that Jesus announces, which is essential for understanding his messianic role. This underscores that God acts in time and space, and that the events he predicts are key elements of his redemptive plan.

19.epoque: The passage is set in a historical context where Jesus is preparing for his crucifixion, a decisive moment for his disciples and for humanity. It is a time of tension and revelation, where Jesus teaches his disciples about faith and divine identity.
19.passage: John 13 takes place during the last meal of Jesus with his disciples, just before his arrest. This chapter is rich in teachings, particularly on service, love, and the revelation of his identity.
19.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, prophetic announcements and declarations of authority were essential for establishing the credibility of a teacher. Jesus uses this context to strengthen the faith of his disciples by revealing truths before they come to pass.
19.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the importance of Jesus' foreknowledge in strengthening the faith of the disciples. By announcing what will happen, he prepares them to believe in him as the Messiah, even in the moments of doubt and confusion that will follow his crucifixion.
19.commentaire: This passage reminds us that faith in Christ is based on his word and promises. By anticipating future events, Jesus invites us to an active trust in him, even when circumstances seem uncertain. We are called to believe not only in what he says but also in who he is, our Savior and Lord.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to send' and is often used in the context of sending a messenger or representative. In the New Testament, it emphasizes the divine authority behind the sending, indicating that the one who is sent carries the message and authority of the one who sends them. Theologically, this reinforces the idea that receiving a messenger from God is, in fact, receiving God himself.

This verb means 'to receive' and implies an active acceptance and warm welcome. In the biblical context, this goes beyond mere physical reception; it is a recognition and opening of the heart toward the one who is sent. Spiritually, this underscores the importance of welcoming the teachings and messengers of God in the believer's life.

This term refers to the one who sends, often in reference to God the Father in the context of sending Jesus and his disciples. This highlights the relationship between the sender and the sent, emphasizing that authority and mission come from God himself. This has a profound theological significance, as it establishes the continuity of divine revelation throughout the ages.

This verb means 'to take' or 'to receive', and in the context of this verse, it implies a reception with faith and commitment. It relates to the idea that receiving a message or a messenger from God involves an active response from the one who receives. Spiritually, this underscores the importance of our response to God's call in our lives.

20.epoque: This verse was spoken during the earthly ministry of Jesus, at a time when relations between Jews and Roman authorities were tense and Jesus' teachings challenged established religious norms.
20.passage: John 13 is set in the context of the last meal of Jesus with his disciples, a moment of deep intimacy and teaching before his crucifixion. This passage emphasizes the importance of the mission of Jesus and his disciples in God's plan.
20.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, welcoming a messenger was an act of great importance, often signifying acceptance of their message and authority. It also reflects the significance of community relationships and hospitality.
20.interpretation: This verse teaches us that receiving a messenger from God is, in fact, welcoming God himself. This underscores the responsibility of believers to recognize and accept those who are sent by God to convey his message.
20.commentaire: This passage reminds us of the importance of our attitude toward those whom God sends into our lives. By welcoming these messengers, we also welcome the presence and authority of God. Therefore, let us be attentive and receptive to the word of God and to those who carry it, for this can transform our understanding and relationship with Him.

mots.sens: This word means 'friend' or 'companion'. It is often used to denote a relationship of closeness and intimacy. In the context of John 13:21, it highlights the betrayal of a close one, making the act even more painful for Jesus. The theological significance here is that even within the community of believers, betrayals can occur, reminding us of the fragility of human relationships.

This term means 'to be troubled' or 'to be agitated'. It expresses a deep emotion, often related to fear or anxiety. In this verse, it reveals the humanity of Jesus, showing that he feels intense pain in light of the impending betrayal. This underscores the depth of his love and commitment to his disciples, even when he knows that one of them will deliver him up.

This word means 'truth'. It is often associated with divine revelation and ultimate reality. In the context of Jesus' statement, it emphasizes the importance of truth in his teachings and relationships. This reminds us that truth, even when painful, is essential for spiritual growth and understanding our human condition.

This term means 'to deliver' or 'to betray'. It is used in the context of handing over a person to an authority or an enemy. In John 13:21, it refers to Judas' betrayal, highlighting the gravity of this act. Theologically, this challenges us to reflect on the nature of sin and how we can sometimes betray our Lord through our actions.

21.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, during the period of Jesus' earthly life, as he teaches and prepares his disciples for his imminent crucifixion.
21.passage: John 13 recounts the last meal of Jesus with his disciples, a crucial moment where he teaches them humility and service while announcing Judas' betrayal.
21.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, the table was a sacred place of communion and friendship. Betraying a friend at this moment was considered one of the greatest betrayals.
21.interpretation: Jesus, troubled in spirit, reveals his humanity in the face of betrayal. This moment highlights the tension between his love for his disciples and the pain of betrayal, calling us to reflect on our own relationships and loyalties.
21.commentaire: This verse reminds us that even in moments of great intimacy, betrayals can occur. It invites us to be vigilant in our relationships and to cultivate authentic fidelity toward Christ and our brothers. By recognizing our own capacity to fail, we are called to seek grace and strength in Jesus to remain faithful in our commitments.

mots.sens: This term refers to disciples or students, those who follow a teacher to learn. In the context of John 13:22, it emphasizes the commitment of the disciples to Jesus, their desire to learn, and their closeness to Him. Spiritually, this reminds us that every believer is called to be a disciple, to listen to and follow the teachings of Christ.

This word means 'one another' and evokes the communal relationship among the disciples. It underscores the importance of fellowship and interaction within the body of Christ. Theologically, this reminds us that the Church is united in faith and that believers must support one another in their walk with God.

This expression means 'they do not know' and reveals the ignorance of the disciples regarding the situation. It highlights their humanity and limitations in understanding divine plans. Spiritually, this teaches us that even in our walk with the Lord, there may be moments of uncertainty where we must trust in His wisdom.

22.epoque: This passage takes place in the 1st century, during Jesus' ministry in Israel, a period marked by religious and political tensions between the Jews and the Romans.
22.passage: John 13 occurs during the Last Supper, a crucial moment before Jesus' crucifixion. The disciples are gathered with Him, and this verse illustrates their confusion regarding the announcement of Judas' betrayal.
22.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, a shared meal was a strong symbol of communion and trust. Betrayal in this context would have been perceived as a particularly heinous act, heightening the tension among the disciples.
22.interpretation: The uncertainty of the disciples regarding the identity of the traitor highlights the difficulty of discerning human heart intentions. This reminds us that even within the community of faith, challenges of trust and understanding can arise.
22.commentaire: This verse teaches us the importance of spiritual vigilance and communion among believers. In our walk with Christ, it is essential to remain attentive to the signs and teachings of our Lord while supporting our brothers and sisters in faith. This encourages us to cultivate authentic relationships based on transparency and love.

mots.sens: This term means 'beloved' and evokes a deep and selfless affection. In the biblical context, it emphasizes the intimate and privileged relationship between Jesus and this disciple, often identified as John. The theological significance of this word highlights Christ's unconditional love for His disciples, a love that transcends mere human relationships.

This verb means 'to lean' or 'to recline.' It evokes a posture of closeness and intimacy. In this verse, it illustrates John's position, who is so close to Jesus, symbolizing a relationship of trust and spiritual communion, essential in the Christian life.

23.epoque: This passage takes place in the 1st century, in a Jewish context under Roman occupation, where social relationships were marked by strict hierarchies and well-established religious traditions.
23.passage: John 13 occurs during the last meal of Jesus with His disciples, a crucial moment before His crucifixion. This chapter highlights themes of humility, service, and love, illustrated by the washing of the feet.
23.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, sitting close to a teacher was a sign of favor and intimacy. It also reflects the structure of meals, where guests reclined around a low table, fostering close exchanges.
23.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the intimacy of the relationship between Jesus and John, representing all believers who are called to draw near to Christ. It reminds us that Jesus' love is accessible to all and that we are called to live in this spiritual closeness.
23.commentaire: This passage invites us to reflect on our own relationship with Jesus. Are we willing to approach Him with confidence and rest in His love? By cultivating this intimacy, we can better understand His will for our lives and live in the fullness of His love.

mots.sens: This word means 'today' and is often used to indicate a present or urgent moment in discourse. In the context of John 13:24, it emphasizes the importance of the moment when Peter seeks to understand Jesus' revelation. Spiritually, this reminds us that every moment with Christ is crucial for our understanding and relationship with Him.

This term means 'sign' or 'indication,' and it is often used to denote something that reveals a deeper truth. In this verse, the sign that Peter asks for is related to the identity of the one who betrays Jesus. Theologically, this teaches us that God uses signs to guide us toward a deeper understanding of His will and plan.

This name, which means 'Yahweh saves,' is central in the New Testament and represents the person of Jesus Christ. In John 13:24, it is crucial to understand that Jesus is the center of divine revelation and redemption. Spiritually, this reminds us that any question we have should be directed toward Him, for He is the source of all truth.

24.epoque: This passage takes place in the context of the 1st century, during the earthly life of Jesus, as He prepares for His crucifixion. The tensions between Jesus and the Jewish religious authorities are at their peak, and His disciples are seeking to understand His mission.
24.passage: John 13 describes the last meal of Jesus with His disciples, an intimate moment where He teaches them profound truths about love and service. This verse highlights the interaction between Peter and Jesus, illustrating the curiosity and concern of the disciples regarding the announcement of betrayal.
24.culture: At that time, meals were moments of communion and sharing, where deep discussions took place. Peter's question underscores the importance of loyalty and betrayal in human relationships, a central theme in the Jewish culture of the time.
24.interpretation: Peter, by asking John to pose the question to Jesus, demonstrates his desire to understand the troubling events unfolding. This teaches us the importance of seeking answers and deepening our understanding of divine revelations, even when the situation seems confusing.
24.commentaire: This verse reminds us that in our moments of perplexity, we must actively seek to understand God's will. Like Peter, we are called to ask questions and draw closer to Jesus for answers. This encourages us not to remain passive in our faith but to engage in dialogue with the Lord to grow in our knowledge of Him.

mots.sens: This word refers to Jesus, the Savior, whose name means 'Yahweh saves.' In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the intimacy and closeness between Jesus and his disciples. The root of the name evokes the idea of deliverance and redemption, thus reinforcing the theological significance of Jesus' presence among his own.

This verb means 'to lean' or 'to incline.' In this passage, it illustrates the act of intimacy and trust of the disciple towards Jesus. This gesture symbolizes a search for revelation and understanding, highlighting the personal relationship that binds the believer to Christ.

This term means 'Lord' and is used to designate an authority or a deity. In this verse, the use of 'Lord' by the disciple testifies to the recognition of Jesus' sovereignty and his central role in divine revelation. It also emphasizes the importance of submission and worship towards Christ.

This word means 'chest' and evokes the idea of closeness and intimacy. By leaning on Jesus' chest, the disciple expresses an affectionate relationship and a quest for knowledge. It also symbolizes vulnerability and the openness of the heart in the face of divine revelation.

25.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, in a Jewish context where interpersonal relationships were marked by strong cultural and religious traditions.
25.passage: John 13 is part of Jesus' farewell discourse, where he prepares his disciples for his impending passion. This moment is crucial as it reveals Jesus' love and closeness to his disciples before his crucifixion.
25.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, sharing a meal was a symbol of intimacy and communion. Leaning on someone's chest was a gesture of trust and affection, highlighting the importance of interpersonal relationships.
25.interpretation: The gesture of the disciple leaning on Jesus' chest symbolizes a quest for truth and a personal relationship with Christ. By asking 'Who is it?', he seeks to understand the looming betrayal while also expressing his attachment to Jesus.
25.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the importance of intimacy with Christ in our spiritual lives. By approaching Him with trust, we can ask our questions and seek answers in His presence. It invites us to cultivate a personal relationship with Jesus, where listening and revelation are essential.

mots.sens: The name 'Ioudas' means 'Jude' and is derived from the Hebrew word 'Yehudah,' which means 'praise.' In the context of the New Testament, it is associated with Judas Iscariot, the disciple who betrayed Jesus. The theological significance of this name highlights the contrast between the praise that Jesus deserves and Judas' betrayal, shedding light on the gravity of his act.

The term 'ἄρτος' refers to bread, a staple food in Jewish culture. In this verse, the dipped bread represents a shared communion and intimacy. Spiritually, it evokes Judas' betrayal, who, despite his closeness to Jesus, chooses to betray him, emphasizing the theme of faithfulness and unfaithfulness in the relationship with God.

The verb 'ἐδίδωμι' means 'to give' and implies an act of generosity or transfer. In this passage, Jesus gives the dipped piece to Judas, symbolizing both a gesture of hospitality and a revelation of the imminent betrayal. Theologically, this underscores Jesus' choice to continue loving even those who betray him, illustrating the depth of his grace.

26.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, during Jesus' ministry in Palestine, a period marked by Roman occupation and religious tensions between the Jews and the Roman authorities.
26.passage: John 13 describes Jesus' last meal with his disciples, where he announces Judas' betrayal. This moment is crucial as it prepares for the events of the crucifixion and illustrates the tension between Jesus' love and the betrayal of one of his close ones.
26.culture: In Jewish culture, sharing a meal, and particularly dipping bread in the dish, was an act of great intimacy and hospitality. This makes Judas' betrayal even more poignant, as he betrays the one with whom he shares a moment of communion.
26.interpretation: This verse highlights Judas' human nature, who, despite his closeness to Jesus, chooses to betray him. Spiritually, it reminds us that even within the Christian community, choices can be made that oppose faithfulness to Christ, calling us to examine our own hearts.
26.commentaire: This passage teaches us about the depth of Jesus' love, who continues to reach out even to those who betray him. It calls us to reflect on our own commitment to Christ and how we can, in turn, manifest unconditional love towards others, even in difficult situations.

mots.sens: This word designates the adversary, the accuser. In the biblical context, it represents not only the enemy of God but also one who seeks to lead men away from the truth. The presence of Satan in this passage underscores the spiritual struggle taking place, where Judas becomes an instrument of betrayal. It reminds believers of the importance of vigilance against temptations.

This verb means 'to enter into' or 'to seize.' It indicates a sudden and decisive action, suggesting that Judas was overtaken by an evil influence. The theological significance here is that the enemy can seize a person when they drift away from God, highlighting the necessity of remaining anchored in faith to resist spiritual attacks.

This verb means 'to do' or 'to act.' In the context of this verse, it is used to urge Judas to carry out his act of betrayal. This raises questions about human responsibility and free will, emphasizing that even though Judas is influenced by Satan, he remains responsible for his actions.

27.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, during Jesus' earthly ministry, in a context where religious and political tensions were high in Judea under Roman occupation.
27.passage: John 13 takes place during Jesus' last meal with his disciples, a crucial moment where he announces his betrayal and prepares his disciples for his imminent death. It is a moment of revelation and spiritual tension.
27.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, sharing a meal symbolized intimacy and trust. Judas' betrayal, in receiving the piece of bread, is all the more shocking and underscores the depth of the betrayal.
27.interpretation: This verse shows how Judas, by accepting the piece of bread, becomes an instrument of Satan, highlighting the struggle between good and evil. Jesus, by telling him to do quickly what he has to do, reveals his knowledge of the upcoming events and his acceptance of the divine plan.
27.commentaire: This passage reminds us of the importance of our choices in the face of temptations. Just like Judas, we can be influenced by external forces, but we have the responsibility for our actions. It is crucial to remain vigilant in our faith and seek God's guidance to avoid falling into spiritual traps.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to understand,' 'to perceive,' or 'to grasp intellectually.' It implies a deep understanding that goes beyond mere recognition. In this context, it highlights the disciples' inability to grasp the spiritual significance of Jesus' words, thus revealing their lack of discernment in the face of the crucial events unfolding around them.

This term refers to a 'table,' often used for meals. In Jewish culture, the table symbolizes communion and intimacy. Here, it represents the place of the Last Supper, where Jesus shares significant moments with his disciples, emphasizing the importance of relationship and unity in the body of Christ.

28.epoque: In the 1st century, Palestine was under Roman rule, and Judaism was experiencing significant religious and political fervor. Messianic expectations were high, and Jesus' disciples were seeking to understand their place in this tumultuous context.
28.passage: John 13 takes place during the Last Supper, a crucial moment where Jesus prepares his disciples for his impending passion. This chapter highlights Jesus' humility in washing his disciples' feet and introduces themes of betrayal and revelation.
28.culture: In Jewish culture, sharing a meal is a sacred act that strengthens community bonds. The disciples, being at the table with Jesus, are confronted with deep truths about loyalty, betrayal, and sacrifice.
28.interpretation: The fact that the disciples do not understand Jesus' words underscores their lack of spiritual preparation for the events to come. This reminds us that spiritual understanding requires a disposition of the heart and an openness to divine teaching.
28.commentaire: This verse invites us to reflect on our own ability to understand God's will in our lives. Like the disciples, we can sometimes be blind to the spiritual truths that God reveals to us. It is essential to pray for a receptive heart and an attentive spirit in order to discern God's voice in our daily lives.

mots.sens: This name refers to Judas Iscariot, one of Jesus' twelve apostles. He is often associated with betrayal, as he delivered Jesus for thirty pieces of silver. In the context of this verse, his role as the group's treasurer highlights an initial trust that will be betrayed, shedding light on human nature and the possibility of deviation even among those close to Christ.

This term means 'will' or 'intention.' In this verse, it is implied that the disciples interpret Jesus' words as a directive for Judas, highlighting their misunderstanding of the situation. This reveals the human tendency to interpret divine actions through a limited lens, often centered on material concerns rather than spiritual ones.

This word translates to 'poor.' It evokes not only an economic condition but also a spiritual dimension, where poverty is often associated with total dependence on God. The mention of the poor in this verse reminds us of the importance of compassion and generosity, central values in Jesus' teaching.

29.epoque: The passage takes place in the 1st century, in the context of Roman-occupied Palestine, where social and religious tensions were palpable.
29.passage: This verse is found in the context of Jesus' last meal with his disciples, a crucial moment before his crucifixion, where he prepares his disciples for his imminent death and the looming betrayal.
29.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, festivals like Passover required specific preparations, and concerns for the poor were often integrated into community life, making the disciples' interpretation all the more significant.
29.interpretation: This verse illustrates the disciples' misunderstanding of Jesus' words, highlighting their inability to grasp the depth of the situation. It brings to light the tension between material concerns and the spiritual truths that Jesus teaches.
29.commentaire: This passage invites us to reflect on our own understanding of God's intentions in our lives. Like the disciples, we can sometimes interpret divine actions through our own concerns, neglecting deep spiritual truths. Let us be attentive to God's voice and his truths, even when they go against our expectations or material desires.

mots.sens: This name refers to Judas Iscariot, one of Jesus' twelve apostles. His name is often associated with betrayal, as he sold Jesus for thirty pieces of silver. In the context of this verse, he represents the deliberate choice to renounce light and truth to plunge into darkness, which has profound implications for human nature and free will.

This verb means 'to hurry' or 'to hasten.' It evokes an urgent and determined action, highlighting Judas' haste to leave Jesus' presence. Spiritually, this can symbolize the quick decision to turn away from light and truth, illustrating how choices can be made in a moment of weakness or distraction.

This term means 'night.' In the Bible, night is often associated with darkness, ignorance, and evil. The mention of night in this verse underscores Judas' transition into a state of spiritual darkness, marking a moment of rupture with the light of Christ and the beginning of his path toward betrayal.

30.epoque: This passage takes place in the 1st century, in the context of Roman-occupied Palestine, a time marked by religious and political tensions.
30.passage: John 13 describes Jesus' last meal with his disciples, a crucial moment where he announces Judas' betrayal. This verse marks the moment when Judas, after receiving the piece of bread, leaves the scene to carry out his act of betrayal.
30.culture: In Jewish culture, sharing bread was an act of communion and trust. The fact that Judas takes the piece of bread before leaving accentuates the gravity of his betrayal against Jesus, who offered him one last opportunity for repentance.
30.interpretation: Judas, by going out into the night, symbolizes the choice of spiritual darkness in the face of the light of Christ. This moment illustrates the struggle between light and darkness, and how choices can lead to tragic consequences.
30.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the importance of our spiritual choices. Just as Judas chose to leave the light for darkness, we are called to remain in the presence of Christ. This encourages us to reflect on our own faithfulness and the decisions we make each day, always seeking to stay close to the truth and divine light.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to glorify' or 'to give glory.' In the context of this verse, it evokes the idea of revealing the greatness and majesty of God. The root of the word is related to the notion of light and splendor, emphasizing that the glorification of Jesus is intrinsically linked to the manifestation of God's divinity. This underscores the theological significance that the glorification of Christ is also that of God, thus revealing their unity in the work of redemption.

This name, which means 'Yahweh saves,' is central in the New Testament. It represents not only the identity of Jesus as Messiah but also his salvific role. In this verse, the name of Jesus is associated with glorification, highlighting that his imminent sacrifice is the means by which salvation is offered to humanity, and that his suffering is the path to divine glory.

The name 'Judas' evokes not only the traitor but also the complexity of the human condition. His act of betrayal is the catalyst that leads to the glorification of Jesus, revealing the paradox of divine sovereignty that uses even evil to accomplish its redemptive plan. This reminds us that even in our failures, God can work for his glory.

31.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the 1st century, during a time when religious and political tensions were high in Israel under Roman occupation.
31.passage: John 13 is part of Jesus' farewell discourse, where he prepares his disciples for his imminent death. Judas' departure marks a crucial turning point in the history of salvation.
31.culture: In Jewish culture, glorification was often associated with victory and the manifestation of divine power. The concept of glory was central to messianic expectations.
31.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the glorification of Jesus is inseparable from his sacrifice. Judas' departure, far from being a random act, is integrated into the divine plan, showing that even human actions can serve to fulfill God's will.
31.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God's glory often manifests through obedience and sacrifice. As believers, we are called to follow Jesus' example, to glorify God in our lives, even in difficult moments. The glorification of Christ encourages us to look beyond immediate circumstances and recognize God's hand at work in our lives.

mots.sens: The verb 'δοξάζω' means 'to glorify' or 'to honor.' In the biblical context, it evokes the idea of paying homage to God's greatness, recognizing his majesty and power. This term is often used to describe how God manifests his glory through his actions and works. Spiritually, it reminds believers that the glorification of God is intrinsically linked to the revelation of his Son, Jesus Christ.

The pronoun 'αὐτός' means 'himself' and is used to emphasize the person concerned. In this verse, it highlights the idea that it is God himself who glorifies Jesus, thus affirming the intimacy and unity between the Father and the Son. Theologically, this reinforces the understanding of Christ's divinity and his central role in the redemptive plan.

The adverb 'σύντομα' means 'soon' or 'quickly.' It indicates a notion of time that is imminent, emphasizing that God's action of glorification towards Jesus is about to be realized. This word invites an active expectation and spiritual preparation for the upcoming events, particularly the crucifixion and resurrection of Christ.

32.epoque: This passage is set in the context of Jesus' ministry in the 1st century, during a time when tensions between the Jewish religious authorities and Jesus were intensifying.
32.passage: John 13 is part of Jesus' farewell discourse, where he prepares his disciples for his imminent passion. This verse emphasizes the glorification of Jesus through his death and resurrection.
32.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, God's glory was often associated with his presence and powerful acts. The glorification of Jesus is therefore a revolutionary concept that redefines the understanding of divine glory.
32.interpretation: This verse reveals that the glorification of Jesus is the result of God's work through him. It emphasizes the idea that Christ's suffering and death are not failures, but means by which God manifests his glory.
32.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God's glory often manifests in moments of suffering and humility. As believers, we are called to look beyond immediate circumstances and recognize that God works for his glory, even in trials. This encourages us to live our faith with confidence, knowing that God will also glorify us in his time.

mots.sens: This word literally means 'little' or 'young.' In the context of John 13:33, Jesus addresses his disciples with paternal tenderness, considering them as his 'little children.' This underscores the intimate and protective relationship he has with them, while announcing his imminent departure, which reinforces their vulnerability and need for spiritual guidance.

This verb means 'to seek' or 'to search for.' In this passage, it evokes a deep and urgent desire to find Jesus, who will soon be taken from them. This highlights the reality of the upcoming separation and the spiritual quest that the disciples will need to undertake to understand Christ's presence even after his ascension.

This relative pronoun means 'where.' In context, it refers to the place where Jesus is going, symbolizing the heavenly nature of his ministry and his return to the Father. This evokes a spiritual dimension of the divine destination, inaccessible to the disciples in the immediate, but which will be revealed later by the Holy Spirit.

33.epoque: This passage is set during the Last Supper, just before Jesus' crucifixion, a pivotal moment in the history of salvation where he prepares his disciples for his imminent departure.
33.passage: John 13 is part of Jesus' farewell discourse, where he teaches and prepares his disciples for his death and the coming of the Holy Spirit, emphasizing the importance of their faith and unity.
33.culture: In Jewish culture, the idea of separation was often associated with loss and suffering, but also with the promise of future redemption. Jesus uses this dynamic to teach his disciples the necessity of faith in physical absence.
33.interpretation: Spiritually, this passage reminds us that even when we cannot see Jesus physically, his presence is always with us through the Holy Spirit. The search for Christ must be constant, even in moments of doubt or separation.
33.commentaire: This verse encourages us to recognize our dependence on Jesus, especially during times of transition and loss. As 'little children,' we are called to actively seek his presence and rely on his promises, knowing that he never abandons us, even when we do not see him.

mots.sens: This term denotes an unconditional and selfless love, often regarded as divine love. It implies a deep commitment to others, without expectation of return. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the requirement of Christian love, which must reflect the love that Christ has for us, a sacrificial and pure love.

This word means 'commandment' and refers to a moral or ethical directive given by an authority. In this verse, it emphasizes that love is not merely an emotion, but a divine imperative, rooted in the will of God. This implies that love must be actively and intentionally practiced by believers.

This term means 'one another' and evokes a community of interdependence and mutual responsibility. It emphasizes that Christian love must be manifested in the relationships among the members of the faith community. This reinforces the idea that love should not be an isolated act but a collective practice within the body of Christ.

34.epoque: In the time of Jesus, Jewish society was marked by religious and cultural tensions, with a strong messianic expectation. Jesus' teachings aimed to reform human relationships by introducing a radical and inclusive love.
34.passage: This passage is set in the context of Jesus' last meal with his disciples, just before his crucifixion. It is part of Jesus' teachings on how his disciples should live and behave after his departure.
34.culture: In Jewish culture, love for one's neighbor was already a fundamental principle, but Jesus elevates this notion by associating it with his own example of sacrificial love. This represents a shift towards a deeper and more demanding love.
34.interpretation: This new commandment emphasizes that Christian love must be the foundation of the community of believers. By loving as Christ has loved, the disciples reflect the nature of God and testify to their identity as Christians.
34.commentaire: This verse reminds us that love is at the heart of the Christian faith. By practicing this unconditional love, we testify to our relationship with Christ and build a strong and united community. Responding to this call requires a daily commitment to actively love our brothers and sisters, even in difficult times.

mots.sens: This term denotes an unconditional and selfless love, often associated with divine love. It is distinguished from other forms of love (such as eros or storgē) by its ability to transcend human emotions and manifest through concrete actions towards others. In this verse, agapē is the foundation of Christian identity, revealing that love among the disciples is the distinguishing mark of their belonging to Christ.

This word means 'disciple' or 'student' and implies a relationship of learning and following. In the biblical context, it is not just about acquiring knowledge, but about living according to the teachings of the master. Being a μαθητής of Christ involves a transformation of life, where love becomes the reflection of faith and commitment to others.

This verb means 'to know' or 'to recognize', and in this context, it refers to a knowledge that goes beyond mere information. It implies a deep and personal recognition of the identity of the disciples through their actions. This knowledge is a powerful testimony of the presence of Christ in the lives of believers, illustrating that their mutual love is a reflection of divine love.

35.epoque: This verse was spoken during the earthly ministry of Jesus, at a time when the disciples faced increasing challenges and persecutions. It was a pivotal moment, just before the crucifixion, where Jesus sought to strengthen unity among his disciples.
35.passage: John 13 is set in the context of Jesus' last meal with his disciples, where he teaches them profound lessons about service, humility, and love. This chapter is crucial as it introduces the new commandment to love others as Christ has loved them.
35.culture: In the first-century Jewish culture, brotherly love and solidarity within the community were fundamental values. By emphasizing mutual love, Jesus redefines and elevates this notion to a spiritual level, associating it with his own sacrifice.
35.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that love among the disciples is not only a commandment but also a testimony of their faith in Christ. Love thus becomes the distinctive mark that identifies true disciples, reflecting the very nature of God.
35.commentaire: The call to love one another is a daily challenge for every Christian. It reminds us that our testimony is not limited to our words, but is manifested in our actions. By cultivating this love, we become ambassadors of Christ in a world that desperately needs to see authentic love.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to follow' and implies an active commitment to following someone. In the context of John 13:36, it emphasizes the idea of discipleship, where the disciple is called to imitate and follow his master. It also reveals the notion of faithfulness and devotion, essential in the relationship between Jesus and his disciples.

This term means 'where' and indicates a specific place or destination. In this verse, it underscores the uncertainty and mystery surrounding Jesus' destination, reinforcing the idea that his disciples cannot fully understand his divine plans at that moment. It also evokes the necessity of faith to follow Christ, even without knowing all the details.

This verb means 'to be about to' or 'to have to'. In this context, it indicates that Peter will follow Jesus at a later time, highlighting God's divine plan and perfect timing. It also underscores Jesus' promise that, despite the current absence, communion will be restored in the future.

36.epoque: This passage is set at the end of Jesus' earthly ministry, just before his crucifixion, in a context of growing tension and anticipation of the upcoming events.
